newsitem.title: BOSNIA: New envoy to Bosnia takes over daunting task.
newsitem.headline: New envoy to Bosnia takes over daunting task.

text.p: Former Spanish U.N. ambassador Carlos Westendorp arrived in Sarajevo on Wednesday to take over as the new international envoy to Bosnia amid concern nationalist leaders are wrecking the peace agreement.
Westdendorp follows former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt, who served 18 months as High Representative to Bosnia overseeing the civilian side of the Dayton peace agreement.
Westendorp held talks with members of the collective presidency in the capital and was scheduled to meet the president of the country's Serb entity, Biljana Plavsic, later in Banja Luka.

Diplomats say the new High Representative takes over against a backdrop of political paralysis in the central government and persistent attempts by indicted war criminal and former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic to obstruct the Dayton accords.
Western powers this week were lobbying Serb leaders to back a customs law and other economic legislation to clear the way for a fund-raising conference for reconstruction aid scheduled on June 24.
If the Serbs refuse, the United States and European governments are contemplating holding the donors' conference without Serb representatives or postponing it.
Bildt, who formally hands over his post to Westendorp on Thursday, has warned that war could erupt again if NATO-led peacekeeping troops leave as scheduled in one year.
Westendorp got his first taste of Bosnia's hostile political climate during a photo session with members of the three-man presidency on Wednesday morning.
The presidency members were asked to pose for a photo with the Moslem chairman, Alija Izetbegovic, standing in the centre, flanked by his Serb and Croat counterparts.

But the Serb member, hardline nationalist Momcilo Krajisnik, objected to his wartime enemy standing in the centre and demanded that Westendorp and Bildt stand between the presidency members instead of behind them.

In previous meetings, Krajisnik -- who accuses Bosnian Moslems of trying to dominate the new central government -- has refused to sit down with presidency members at a rectangular table, diplomats say.
Krajisnik has insisted on meeting at a circular table to symbolise "equality" among the three presidency members.
